source: Parashar et al. (2025) Inference-Time Computations for LLM Reasoning and Planning: A Benchmark and Insights (Sys2Bench)
finding: Independent benchmark of CoT, SC@5, ToT and RAP on 11 tasks and 5 models (Llama 8B/70B/405B, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o). ToT often loses to plain CoT or SC on arithmetic and logic; it wins big on Game of 24; planning is mixed. No method is best everywhere.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-4o: CoT 94.7, SC@5 94.9, ToT 93.5. ProntoQA GPT-4o: CoT 91.8, SC 91.4, ToT 32.8. Game of 24 GPT-4o: CoT 14, SC 18, ToT 62; Llama 405B ToT 69. Blocksworld Llama 405B: CoT 48.7, SC 52.1, ToT 19.9; GPT-4o ToT 12.4 vs CoT 37.5. HotPotQA GPT-4o: SC 52.6, ToT 38.2. Llama 8B GSM8K tokens: CoT about 1.9e4, RAP about 9.9e6 for +7.5 points.
quote: Tree search struggles with increasing complexity, performing significantly worse than CoT
limits: SC@5 is not token-matched to ToT; ToT is a re-implementation by the benchmark authors; Rubik's cube near 0 for all. No frontier reasoning model with ToT.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 1 and 6: on a 2024-25 model (GPT-4o) a prompt-only tree helps only on checkable puzzle-like tasks and hurts on logic and planning. Gate S6 search by task type.

source: Parashar et al. (2025) Sys2Bench Table 3, large reasoning models with plain prompting
finding: Plain-prompted o1 and o1-mini beat the tree and sampling methods run on weaker models on most tasks, so the reasoning model already does the search internally.
numbers: o1 / o1-mini IO: Game of 24 73 / 77; Blocksworld 99.2 / 48.3; Trip Plan 58.3 / 24.0; GSM8K 98 / 98; Binpacking 99 / 90; Rubik's cube 0.6 / 0. Compare GPT-4o ToT: Game of 24 62, Blocksworld 12.4, Trip Plan 19.5.
limits: Cross-model comparison, not ToT on top of o1. Rubik's cube stays near 0 even for o1.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly answered: a reasoning model without a tree beats a non-reasoning model with a tree. Whether a tree adds to a reasoning model is still untested here.

source: Drori et al. (2025) Diverse Inference and Verification for Advanced Reasoning
finding: Wrapping reasoning models (o3-mini high, o1) in outer search or sampling methods raises accuracy on hard sets. Best-of-N gave the biggest gain on HLE, MCTS also helped. Combining 8 diverse methods lifted IMO combinatorics from 3/9 (best single) to 7/9.
numbers: HLE 100-question sample: o3-mini high 13.0; +SC(N=5) 18; +MoA(N=3) 19; +LEAP 23; +MCTS(N=2) 28; +Best-of-N(N=3) 37. IMO combinatorics 9 problems: o1 zero-shot 1/9, best single method 3/9, 8 methods 6/9 (o1) and 7/9 (o3-mini high). ARC 400 puzzles: 53% to 69.5% without o3; o3 91.5% to 93.75%.
quote: verification is simple and effective for math and code
limits: Tiny samples (100 HLE, 9 IMO). Cost over $1 per question per method. HLE selection is by answer agreement, not a checker. Verifier is Lean or code on IMO and ARC. R1 only as baseline. Outer search, not ToT proper.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9: outer sampling and method diversity do add on top of reasoning models, mostly when a checker exists. Method diversity beats one method. Treat as a hypothesis for S6 on a reasoning model.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Evolving Deeper LLM Thinking (Mind Evolution)
finding: Prompt-only evolutionary search (LLM generates, recombines, refines) beats Best-of-N and sequential revision at the same 800-candidate cap on natural-language planning, when a programmatic evaluator scores candidates.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash. TravelPlanner: 1-pass 5.6, Best-of-N 55.6, Sequential-Revision+ 82.8, Mind Evolution 95.6 (100 with Pro fallback). Trip planning 20.6/77.2/74.4/96.2. Meeting planning 20.8/69.4/62.0/85.0. StegPoet 0/1.0/19.8/46.5. TravelPlanner cost per problem: ME $0.29, BoN $0.47, SeqRev+ $2.75.
limits: All evaluators are programmatic; an LLM evaluator was not tested ('can be noisy'). Authors ran their own baselines.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a prompt-only search beats equal-budget sampling on a 2025 model, but only with a hard checker. Without a checker it is unproven.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning in Natural Language Improves LLM Search for Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Searching over natural-language plans (ideas) before code beats repeated sampling at equal sample count. Gain tracks idea diversity. It can hurt pass@1.
numbers: LiveCodeBench pass@200: Claude-3.5-Sonnet RS 55.6, IdeaSearch 70.2, PlanSearch 77.0; GPT-4o 60.6/70.4/73.0; GPT-4o-mini 53.3/59.4/64.9. o1-mini 90.8/91.2/91.3 (almost no gain). HumanEval+ GPT-4o 98.2/97.6/99.5. Tokens per problem: RS about 244 per sample, PlanSearch about 1,428; PlanSearch only pulls ahead around 10,000 tokens.
limits: Matched by sample count, not tokens at small budgets. Uses tests for filtering; checkable task. o1-mini gets little from search.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: search at plan level works on non-reasoning models; a reasoning model (o1-mini) gains 0.5 points. Idea-level diversity is the lever, which fits an idea tree at S6.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) climbs steadily with samples, but picking the right answer without a checker fails: majority vote and a reward model plateau near 100 samples.
numbers: MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward-model pick only 40.50% to 41.41%. CodeContests Gemma-2B 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000. SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250.
quote: majority voting and reward models do not possess this ability
limits: Models are small. Coverage is an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the value or pick step is the bottleneck. Search width only helps if the scorer can find the rare right branch. Add a checker wherever one exists.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Inference Scaling Laws: Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem Solving
finding: With a trained reward model, the tree method REBASE beats plain sampling at equal compute, and MCTS does not. A small model with the better search can match a model 8x larger.
numbers: Llemma-7B REBASE 46.8% MATH500 at 1.48e14 FLOPs vs Llemma-34B sampling 46.7% at 12.1e14. Mistral-7B 256-sample sampling 42.8 (8.70e14) vs REBASE 32 samples 45.0 (1.36e14). MCTS below sampling at every budget on MATH. Greedy MATH 28.6 to 33.0.
limits: Needs a trained process reward model. In Table 4 REBASE uses 16-41% more FLOPs at equal samples. Math only; 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: simple balanced branching beats elaborate MCTS, but only with a trained scorer. A prompt-only scorer version is untested.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (re-opened for difficulty rules)
finding: Best split of compute depends on difficulty. Easy: sequential revisions. Hard: a balance of sequential and parallel. Beam search with a PRM wins at low budget on medium-hard items and hurts on easy ones at high budget.
numbers: Compute-optimal matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (16 vs 64 generations for search; 64 vs 256 for revisions). Beats a 14x larger model only on easy and medium questions or low inference load; on hard questions pretraining wins. Level 5 questions: no method progresses.
limits: Difficulty bins need the base model's pass rate over 2048 samples, or a PRM. Not available at deployment without cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: usable rule: easy items go sequential (revise), medium-hard go branching, hardest do not pay. Difficulty must be estimated cheaply, for example by agreement among 3-5 samples.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning
finding: Stopping the voting early when answers already agree saves about 3x samples with no accuracy loss. This gives a prompt-only difficulty signal for width.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: 3.2x average sample reduction, accuracy change -0.07%; up to 7.9x. By task: math 3.3x, commonsense 2.9x, symbolic 3.8x, code 2.4x. GPT-3.5 4.4x. Baseline 40 samples; confidence threshold 0.95.
limits: Voting only, not tree search. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: width rule without a trained reward model: sample until agreement passes a threshold, widen only when answers disagree.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: For reasoning models, parallel sampling with early stop on the shortest chains beats full majority voting at lower cost. Longer chains are less accurate within a question.
numbers: Math avg per question, shortest / random / longest accuracy: R1-670B 83.3/78.2/58.9; QwQ-32B 71.1/68.9/56.7; R1-32B 60.0/55.5/37.8; LN-Super-49B 63.4/47.7/28.9. short-1@k matches majority@k with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens; short-3@k beats it by about 2% (QwQ, 80k tokens) and 4% (R1-670B, 100k).
limits: Math only, open reasoning models. Voting, not tree.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: for a reasoning model, cheap parallel samples plus a selection rule already give gains; a tree must beat this baseline.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models
finding: Longer solutions are not more correct in o1-like models; correct solutions are shorter than wrong ones. Majority vote with a shortest tie-break helps unevenly.
numbers: Correct solutions consistently shorter; longest about 2x shortest. 16-sample AIME: R1-Distill-32b MV 72.88, Shortest MV 73.77; 14b 71.77 vs 71.55; QwQ 51.33 vs 50.88; LIMO 68.88 vs 70.00.
limits: Gain is not uniform across models. Small test sets.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: more internal thinking can hurt, so an external tree that lengthens the chain needs a length-aware stop.

source: Naik et al. (2023) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (Div-Se)
finding: Prompting the same model with several different solution approaches beats self-consistency at equal cost.
numbers: GPT-4 Blocksworld 4/5: CoT 40.0, SC-10 41.2, Div-Se 69.6. Graph coloring: CoT 15, SC-10 23, Div-Se 97. GPT-3.5 AQuA: CoT 59.0, SC-5 63.4, Div-Se 72.8. GSM8K GPT-4 near ceiling (94-95), small gain.
quote: for a fixed cost, our approaches always give better performance
limits: Text and table disagree on a few gains. Cost matching is by the authors. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (generator side): vary the approach per branch rather than resampling the same prompt.

source: Panickssery et al. (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models prefer their own output, and the preference grows with how well they recognise it. A model scoring its own thoughts is biased upward.
numbers: 1000 articles each from XSUM and CNN/DM. GPT-4 recognises itself 73.5%. Self-preference out of the box: GPT-4 0.705 (XSUM), 0.912 (CNN). Swapping source labels cut GPT-4 XSUM from 0.73 to 0.32. Kendall tau of recognition vs preference 0.41-0.82 for GPT-3.5. Order flips: GPT-4 25%, GPT-3.5 58%, Llama 89%.
limits: Summarisation, not reasoning. Causality shown only by fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: scoring thoughts with the model that wrote them inflates scores. Use a different model, or blind, order-randomised scoring.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing Judges with Juries: Evaluating LLM Generations with a Panel of Diverse Models (PoLL)
finding: A panel of three small models from different families agrees with humans more than one GPT-4 judge, shows less self-bias, and costs 7-8x less.
numbers: Cohen kappa vs human: NQ GPT-4 0.627, PoLL 0.763; TriviaQA 0.841 vs 0.906; HotpotQA 0.830 vs 0.867 (Haiku alone 0.873). Chatbot Arena Pearson 0.817 vs 0.917, Kendall 0.667 vs 0.778. Spread of deviation on multi-hop: PoLL 2.2, GPT-3.5 6.1. GPT-4 kappa on NQ ranged 0.518 to 0.725 by prompt.
limits: QA and pairwise chat judging; not thought scoring in a search. Panel is Command R, Haiku, GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: scorer diversity helps for judging in this setting. Not tested inside a tree.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study
finding: On idea tasks an LLM judge barely beats chance at picking the ideas humans rate better. Over-generation yields few distinct ideas.
numbers: Best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise) 53.3% agreement with human consensus; GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%; random 50%; human reviewers among themselves 56.1%. Of 4,000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 (5%) were non-duplicates. AI ideas rated more novel: 5.64 vs 4.84 human (n=109 vs 119 reviews, p<0.01).
limits: Human reviewers are noisy too (56.1%). Research ideas in NLP only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: on uncheckable idea tasks a prompt-only scorer is near chance. An idea tree needs dedup and external ranking; width alone yields duplicates.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: Expert writers rate LLM stories 3-10x less likely to pass creativity tests than New Yorker stories. The abstract says no LLM judge correlates positively with experts.
numbers: 48 stories (12 New Yorker, 36 LLM), 10 experts, about 2,016 binary labels. Pass rate New Yorker 84.7%, Claude v1.3 30.0%, GPT-4 27.9%, GPT-3.5 8.7%. Expert Fleiss kappa mean 0.41 (0.27-0.66).
limits: The full LLM-vs-expert table was in the unread part of the page; the correlation claim is from the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: independent-judge evidence says LLM judges of creative writing do not track experts, so Yao's GPT-4 judge result (K23) is weak support. I found no independent ToT creative-writing replication.

source: Liu et al. (2023) LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency
finding: Letting the LLM translate the problem into PDDL and handing it to a classical planner beats LLM planning and an LLM ToT planner, but only when the domain is formalisable and a worked example is given.
numbers: 20 tasks per domain, 7 domains. Success LLM+P vs LLM-as-planner vs ToT: Blocksworld 90 / 15 / 0; Grippers 95 / 35 / 10; Storage 85 / 0 / 0; Barman 20 / 0 / 0; Floortile 0 / 0 / 0; Termes 20 / 0 / 0; Tyreworld 10 (90 incl. suboptimal) / 15 / 0. Without the example problem LLM+P scores 0 everywhere.
quote: fail to recognize when a plan reaches the goal
limits: GPT-4; the ToT baseline times out because of many calls. LLM+P failures are mis-specified problem files.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: formal code beats per-node LLM calls where a domain model exists. The share of our tasks that can be formalised is small; others need the LLM tree.

source: Silver et al. (2024) Generalized Planning in PDDL Domains with Pretrained Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 writes a Python program for a whole planning domain, which then solves unseen tasks fast. A debugging loop is essential and results are all-or-nothing by domain.
numbers: 7 PDDL domains, 10 seeds, 30 eval tasks per seed. GPT-4 solved fraction: Delivery 0.90, Forest 1.00, Gripper 0.90, Ferry 0.80, Heavy 0.60, Spanner 0.10, Miconic 0.01. Without debugging Delivery 0.10. GPT-3.5 near 0. Error types: Python exception 40%, plan semantics 34%, syntax 13%, timeout 13%.
limits: Run through the ChatGPT web interface. With meaningless PDDL names most domains drop to 0-0.11.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: code-as-successor works when names carry meaning and tests exist, and fails on structure the model misses. Always keep a test-and-debug loop.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP), re-opened for ablation
finding: RAP has no ablation that separates the state rewrite (world model) from branching in the text I read. It does ablate reward terms, and effects are task-bound.
numbers: GSM8K LLaMA-33B: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP(1) 40.0, RAP(10) 48.6, +aggregation 51.6. Blocksworld RAP(10) 100/86/26 at 2/4/6 steps.
quote: the action likelihood reward is essential for plan generation, but not very helpful to mathmatical reasoning
limits: Appendix F reward tables not read. RAP(1) vs CoT (+10.6) hints that structure, not breadth, gives part of the gain, but SC(10) gives +17.4 at 10x cost. Inference only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Indirect signal only. Run our own test: tree with and without state rewrite.

source: Bi et al. (2024) Forest-of-Thought, re-opened for baselines and compute
finding: FoT numbers are the authors' own; baselines are not stated as re-run; no equal-token table in the text.
numbers: Game of 24, 95 problems: ToT b=5 74.00% at 13.74 calls; FoT 96.84% at 25.64 calls (about 1.9x ToT calls); XoT 85.40% at 1.78 calls. Llama3-8B ablation: base 10.58, +self-correction 60.24, +input enhancement 77.98. MATH500/AIME: Qwen2.5-7B 82.6/6.0; FoT n=8 86.2/46.67; QwQ 90.6/50.0; FoT n=4 on QwQ 91.2/53.3.
limits: Only call counts, no tokens. Equal-cost claim sits in a figure. I found no third-party run.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. FoT gains partly come from added self-correction and input enhancement, not trees alone. On QwQ the gain is small (+0.6 MATH500, +3.3 AIME), echoing gap 2.
